title: AP Reports Epstein Files Disappeared from DOJ Public Website
description_short: AP Reports Epstein Files Disappeared from DOJ Public Website
description_medium: Associated Press reporters found that at least 16 Epstein-related files disappeared from the Justice Department’s public webpage less than a day after posting. The files were available Friday and unavailable Saturday. DOJ did not explain the individual removals, but said materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted. This establishes a change in public website availability, not deletion of original records or shortened oversight.
description_long: On December 20, 2025, The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files posted to the Justice Department’s public Epstein-documents webpage the previous day were no longer accessible by Saturday. AP described several missing images, including one that showed a photograph of Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump, and Ghislaine Maxwell inside a drawer. The department did not answer AP’s questions about the specific files. In a public statement, DOJ said that photographs and other materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted under the law as it received additional information. That statement gives a general review rationale, not a file-by-file explanation. The documented event is the disappearance of material from a public webpage after release. The report does not establish that DOJ destroyed originals, that records were permanently deleted, or that any oversight window was compressed. Those broader claims should be excluded unless supported by separate records.
notes: Focused read of the linked Associated Press URL returned HTTP 403, so the article text and its file-level evidence could not be checked. The supplied synopsis says the report identified Epstein-related files missing from a Justice Department webpage. It does not name the files or URLs, give removal dates or page-history records, quote DOJ’s explanation, or identify an oversight decision affected; it also does not establish deletion of original records or a shortened oversight period.

description_long: The U.K. public inquiry into Alexander Litvinenko’s death provides a documented account of the press conference held in Moscow on November 17, 1998. It says Litvinenko went public with criticism of the Federal Security Service (FSB), and that former colleague Vladimir Trepashkin and several other officers were also present. The inquiry also reports that the conference received widespread media coverage and that Litvinenko and the involved officers were dismissed from the FSB in December 1998. title: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
description_short: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that the new administration took down the White House Spanish-language website within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration; the Spanish-language X profile @LaCasaBlanca and a reproductive-freedom page were also disbanded. A White House spokesperson said the site was being edited and that archived content had gone dormant, and said the translation section would return. The evidence supports unavailability during the transition, not a permanent deletion claim.
description_long: Within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration, the White House Spanish-language homepage became unavailable and showed an error page. The Associated Press reported the change the next day and identified @LaCasaBlanca, the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, and a government reproductive-freedom page as also disbanded. When asked about the changes, White House principal deputy press secretary Harrison Fields said the administration was developing and editing the website, that some archived content had gone dormant, and that it was committed to bringing the Spanish translation section back online. AP also noted that Trump had removed a Spanish White House page in 2017 and that the Biden administration restored it in 2021. These details distinguish the observed outage and account removals from an established permanent shutdown: the administration described the website status as transition work and promised restoration, though the report did not specify a date. The corrected entry should say the services went offline during the transition and include the administration’s stated explanation. It should not claim all Spanish-language government accounts were permanently deleted.

title: U.S.–Saudi Nuclear Deal Omits IAEA Additional Protocol, Arms-Control Group Says
description_short: U.S.–Saudi Nuclear Deal Omits IAEA Additional Protocol, Arms-Control Group Says
description_medium: The Arms Control Association’s September 2026 review says the U.S.–Saudi civil nuclear agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA Additional Protocol; instead, the deal uses a bilateral safeguards agreement limited to covered sites. The review notes that this arrangement includes short-notice IAEA inspections at covered sites but offers less access to undeclared locations. The evidence supports a safeguards-scope concern, not a claim that all IAEA safeguards were bypassed.
description_long: The Arms Control Association’s September 1, 2026 analysis of the U.S.–Saudi civil nuclear cooperation agreement says the deal does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA Additional Protocol. Instead, it relies on a U.S.–Saudi bilateral safeguards agreement implemented by the IAEA and limited to facilities covered by the nuclear cooperation agreement. The Association says the bilateral arrangement includes some measures beyond Saudi Arabia’s standard comprehensive safeguards agreement, including short-notice inspections at covered sites, but does not provide the broader access to undeclared sites and activities available under the Additional Protocol. The IAEA’s country factsheet independently lists Saudi Arabia’s safeguards agreement under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty as in force since January 13, 2009. The Arms Control Association assesses the narrower bilateral agreement as insufficient to assure the absence of undeclared nuclear activity; that is the organization’s expert assessment, not an IAEA finding that safeguards were bypassed. A precise entry should describe the omission of the Additional Protocol and the criticism of the substitute agreement, while acknowledging the safeguards that remain and attributing the evaluation.
notes: Worker 22 evidence resolution: Nuclear cooperation alone does not prove that IAEA safeguards are weakened or bypassed. The linked AP article could not be reviewed in the source pass, and the record lacks agreement text, inspection terms, and attributable warnings from named officials. Do not state the alleged safeguard effect as fact.
Worker 22 follow-up: The agreement does not eliminate all IAEA safeguards; the bilateral agreement covers designated sites.

title: Trump Fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper After 2020 Election
description_short: Trump Fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper After 2020 Election
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Donald Trump fired Defense Secretary Mark Esper on November 9, 2020, one week after the presidential election. Trump announced the change on Twitter and said National Counterterrorism Center director Christopher Miller would become acting secretary, bypassing Deputy Secretary David Norquist. AP described the decision as unprecedented and connected it to Trump’s post-election conflict with Esper; no military operation consequence is established by this account.
description_long: On November 9, 2020, one week after the presidential election, President Donald Trump announced that Defense Secretary Mark Esper was leaving the job effective immediately. The Associated Press reported that Trump said National Counterterrorism Center director Christopher Miller would serve as acting secretary, rather than Deputy Secretary David Norquist, the department’s second-ranking official. AP characterized the firing as an unprecedented move by a president struggling to accept the election result and angry at a Pentagon leader he viewed as insufficiently loyal. That characterization is AP’s reporting, not a formal explanation issued in a dismissal order. The event-specific report supports the dismissal date, the immediate acting appointment, and the unusual bypass of the deputy secretary. It does not show that the change altered a particular military operation or policy, and this proposal makes no such claim. The supplied Guardian URL did not provide readable text in the earlier check, so the corrected account relies on the AP report carried by PBS NewsHour and confines the description to the personnel change and documented transition.

description_long: The Department of Justice Office of the Pardon Attorney’s official table of commutations granted by Donald Trump places Matthew Antione Canady under January 19, 2021. It identifies the Southern District of Iowa case and records a 262-month term of imprisonment, as amended by a December 22, 2014 order, followed by five years of supervised release. The listed offense is conspiracy to distribute at least 50 grams of cocaine base. This verifies that Canady appears on the administration’s commutations list and identifies the underlying sentence; it does not give the replacement prison term, whether the commutation was to time served, a release date, or the remaining supervision terms. The linked clemency-record PDF should be inspected for those details before describing the practical effect. A commutation changes punishment but is distinct from a pardon of the conviction. The corrected account can state the grant and original case facts while clearly noting that the public summary alone does not quantify the relief. It should not imply that Canady’s conviction was erased or that the commutation resulted in immediate release.
